questions.prompt: Per Lesson 2, what is Azure AI Foundry (the portal reachable at ai.azure.com)?
options: A single portal combining a model catalog, interactive playgrounds, build-and-customize tools, and assess-and-improve tooling for AI models and agents
A dedicated, hourly-billed virtual machine that a model runs on
An API that screens prompts and responses for harmful content across four harm categories
A CLI command that lists the GPU VM sizes actually available in a given Azure region
A reserved-capacity billing model for predictable, high-volume Azure OpenAI traffic
A private network interface that gives an Azure resource a private IP address inside a VNet
questions.explain: Azure AI Foundry's portal at ai.azure.com does four jobs: a model catalog for browsing and deploying models, interactive playgrounds for testing before writing code, build-and-customize tools like fine-tuning and agent configuration, and assess-and-improve tooling like tracing and evaluation. It has been called Azure AI Studio and is now officially Microsoft Foundry, but the portal and its four jobs are unchanged.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B describes managed compute, one of the three deployment options the Foundry portal lets you choose from — a dedicated VM you size and pay for by the hour. Managed compute is something you configure through Foundry; it isn't what Foundry itself is. Foundry is the catalog-plus-playgrounds-plus-tooling portal that covers deployment, testing, building, and assessment generally, not any one deployment option.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a cloud AI platform bundles four things that are each expensive to build yourself — elastic compute, a model catalog, governance, and one ________.
questions.explain: Lesson 1 lists elastic compute, a model catalog, governance, and one bill (pay per token or per deployment-hour, instead of owning depreciating hardware) as the four things a cloud AI platform bundles together that would each be expensive to build and operate yourself.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the three paths to production from Lesson 1.
options: Self-hosted means you own every patch, driver update, and scaling decision forever
A cloud AI platform is a provider that runs the model (or hosts it for you) while you call an API
A fully managed SaaS product still requires you to make infrastructure decisions, just more automated ones
This course centers on the self-hosted path, since that's where most AI engineering jobs sit
A cloud AI platform bundles elastic compute, a model catalog, governance, and one bill
questions.explain: Self-hosting means owning every operational decision indefinitely. A cloud AI platform runs or hosts the model behind an API call, bundling elastic compute, a model catalog, governance, and one bill. Fully managed SaaS is the third path, and it deliberately removes infrastructure decisions entirely rather than just automating them. This course centers on the cloud AI platform path, not self-hosting, because that's where most AI engineering jobs actually sit.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its meaning, per Lesson 1.
right: A billing model based on usage rather than owned hardware
You own and operate the GPU infrastructure and serving stack
A single platform's curated list of available models from multiple providers
A managed service that runs models behind an API
questions.explain: Self-hosted means owning the GPU infrastructure and serving stack yourself. A cloud AI platform is a managed service running models behind an API. A model catalog is one platform's curated list of available models. Pay-per-token is a usage-based billing model, the opposite of owning depreciating hardware.

questions.prompt: A team upgrades the underlying model behind the deployment named my-support-bot-prod from GPT-4o to GPT-4.1, per Lesson 3. What has to change in the application code shown above?
options: Nothing — Azure OpenAI routes requests by deployment name, not model name, so the same code keeps working
The model parameter must be updated to "gpt-4.1" at every call site
The resource's API key must be regenerated before the new model will respond
The deployment must be renamed to include the new model's name
questions.explain: Azure OpenAI routes requests by deployment name, a name you chose yourself when you deployed the model, not by the underlying model's own name. Swapping which model powers a given deployment name, like upgrading my-support-bot-prod from GPT-4o to GPT-4.1, doesn't require touching any call site, as long as the deployment name itself doesn't change.

questions.prompt: Put these three names for the same Azure AI portal in the order Lesson 2 says they were used, oldest to newest.
items: Azure AI Studio — the original name, retired
Azure AI Foundry — what most documentation and this course's lesson titles still call it
Microsoft Foundry — the current official name as of 2026
questions.explain: Lesson 2 traces one product through three names: it started as Azure AI Studio, was renamed Azure AI Foundry (still the most common name in documentation, job listings, and this course), and is now officially Microsoft Foundry as of 2026 — the portal URL and underlying service never changed, only the brand.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 8, what does Azure AI Search's Import data wizard actually do?
options: It builds an index, an indexer, and a data source connection together in one no-code pass
It fine-tunes a chat model on the documents stored in a search index
It grants a managed identity Storage Blob Data Reader access to a storage account automatically
It scores moderated content by severity across four harm categories
It lists the number of indexes, indexers, and data sources already used against a service's free-tier quota
It routes 100% of inference traffic to a newly created model deployment
questions.explain: The Import data wizard, launched from the Azure AI Search service's Overview page, builds an index, an indexer, and a data source connection all in one pass, instead of configuring each one separately through code or the REST API. It's specifically the no-code path to a working RAG search setup.
questions.distractorExplain: Option E describes the Usage link on the service's Overview page — checking capacity against the free tier's limit of three indexes, three indexers, and three data sources — which Lesson 8 says to check BEFORE using Import data. It's a related, earlier step, but it's a capacity check, not the wizard that actually builds the index, indexer, and data source together.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: ________ tries several authentication methods in order — your Azure CLI login, a managed identity, environment variables — until one works, so the same code authenticates correctly on your laptop and in production with no key hardcoded.
questions.explain: DefaultAzureCredential tries multiple authentication methods in order until one succeeds, which is exactly why the same code block works unchanged on a developer's laptop (via az login) and in production (via managed identity) without ever hardcoding a key.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about deploying a model from the Foundry catalog, per Lesson 7.
options: Models sold directly by Microsoft deploy immediately, with no terms-and-conditions step
Models from partners and community show a terms step only the first time they're deployed in a given project
Managed compute deployments ask you to choose instance count and VM size yourself
Foundry always picks the deployment's connection automatically, with no way to change it
Provisioning state and deployment state both have to be checked, but they tell you two different things
questions.explain: Microsoft's own models deploy immediately, while partner and community models show a one-time-per-project terms step. Managed compute specifically asks you to size the hardware (instance count, VM size), unlike the other two deployment options. Foundry auto-selects a connection by default, but a Customize option lets you change it when you have a specific reason to. Provisioning state confirms the resource itself was created, while deployment state confirms the model inside it is actually healthy and serving — two different checks, not one.

questions.prompt: A content moderation call returns a severity score of 4 (Medium) for the Hate and fairness category, per Lesson 9. What does that score represent?
options: Offensive, demeaning, or harmful-instruction content — more severe than low-intensity offensive language, but short of explicit or illegal harm
Content that every application must reject outright, regardless of configuration
A score that only applies to image content, never text
Content considered fine for general, journalistic, or professional contexts
questions.explain: Content Safety scores severity per category on a 0/2/4/6 scale: Safe (0), Low (2), Medium (4), High (6). A Medium score means offensive, demeaning, or harmful-instruction content — worse than the opinionated, low-intensity language of a Low score, but not yet the explicit, severe, or illegal harm of a High score. What severities an application actually accepts is configured per application, not fixed by the score itself.

questions.prompt: Match each piece of an Azure AI Search RAG setup to what it does, per Lesson 8.
right: Supports keyword, vector, and hybrid search at request time
Where your content actually lives, such as Azure Blob Storage
A searchable copy of your content, with defined, typed fields
Automates pulling content from a data source into the index
questions.explain: An index is the searchable, typed copy of your content. An indexer automates loading a data source into that index. The data source is where the content actually lives, most commonly Blob Storage or Data Lake Storage Gen2. The query engine supports keyword, vector, and hybrid search once the index exists.

questions.prompt: Put these three layers of AI service monitoring in the order Lesson 11 introduces them.
items: Operational metrics — token usage, latency, and run success rate
Evaluation metrics — coherence, fluency, groundedness, and safety scores
Tracing — the full execution path of a single request, end to end
questions.explain: Lesson 11 covers three layers of visibility: operational metrics (the same categories tracked for any production service), evaluation metrics (quality scores run against a sample of real traffic), and tracing (the complete execution path of one request, including every LLM call, tool invocation, and agent decision).

questions.prompt: A team needs to fine-tune a model too large to fit on a single GPU, spreading it across multiple GPUs in one VM. Per Lesson 12, which Azure GPU VM family is actually built for that?
options: ND-series
NC-series
NV-series
A CPU-only VM size, since fine-tuning doesn't require a GPU
questions.explain: NC-series is the default starting point for general AI/ML training and inference, but ND-series specifically exists for models too large for a single GPU, spreading the workload across multiple GPUs per VM. NV-series is tuned for visualization and virtual desktops, not training, despite also having a GPU.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: before committing a compute budget to a specific GPU VM size, ________ lists every size of that series actually sellable in a given Azure region right now.
questions.explain: Running az vm list-skus with a --location and --size filter is a cheap sanity check against designing an architecture around a SKU that turns out to be unavailable or on backorder in that specific region, since GPU capacity varies by region and is scarcer than regular compute.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about securing an AI endpoint's network access, per Lesson 14.
options: Disabling public access alone also cuts off your own app's legitimate traffic, until a private endpoint is in place
A private endpoint gets its own network interface inside your own VNet, with a private IP address
A private endpoint connection has to be approved on the original resource before traffic flows through it
Disabling public access changes the shape of the SDK calls and authentication your application code uses
Only resources inside the VNet, or connected to it through peering or a VPN, can reach the service through a private endpoint
questions.explain: Turning off public access blocks everyone, including your own app, until a private endpoint exists. That private endpoint is its own NIC with a private IP inside your VNet, reachable only from inside that network (or through peering/VPN), and the connection itself has to be explicitly approved on the original resource before any traffic flows. None of this changes the API itself — the SDK calls and authentication look identical either way; only the network path changes.

questions.prompt: An engineer writes an autoscale rule that scales a GPU-based model-serving VM up and down purely on CPU utilization. Per Lesson 15, why is that the wrong metric to scale on?
options: Because an AI inference endpoint's real bottleneck is usually GPU utilization, queue depth, or token throughput — rarely the CPU
Because Azure Autoscale doesn't support CPU as a metric at all
Because a scale rule's duration can never be set below 10 minutes
Because manual scale is mandatory for any resource with an attached GPU
questions.explain: A typical web app's bottleneck is CPU or concurrent requests, which is why Autoscale offers those metrics by default. A GPU-based inference endpoint's bottleneck is rarely the CPU — it's GPU utilization, how deep the request queue is getting, or tokens-per-second throughput — so a rule has to target what's actually saturated, not whatever metric happens to be easiest to read out of the box.

questions.prompt: Match each term to what it actually is, per Lessons 14 and 16.
right: Explicitly grants a registered identity permission to reach a resource like Key Vault — nothing is reachable by default
An Azure-managed credential with no secret for a developer to handle or leak
Gives a resource a private IP address inside your own VNet, reachable only from inside that network
A managed identity tied to one specific resource's lifecycle, deleted along with that resource
questions.explain: A managed identity is an Azure-managed credential with nothing for a developer to leak. A private endpoint gives a resource a private IP inside your own VNet. A system-assigned identity is specifically tied to one resource's own lifecycle. And an identity on its own can't reach anything — an access policy or RBAC role assignment is what explicitly grants it permission to reach something like Key Vault.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of locking an AI endpoint down to private-only access in the correct order, per Lesson 14.
items: Disable public access on the resource's Networking tab
Create a private endpoint with its own NIC inside your VNet
Approve the pending private endpoint connection back on the original resource
Confirm the resource is now reachable only from inside the VNet
questions.explain: Disabling public access comes first, but on its own it would cut off legitimate traffic too. Creating a private endpoint gives the resource a private IP inside your VNet, but the connection still shows up waiting for approval on the original resource — nothing passes through it until that approval happens. Only after all three steps is the resource reachable exclusively from inside the VNet.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 17, what does AWS Bedrock's Converse API actually provide, compared to calling five different model providers' own native SDKs directly?
options: One unified request/response shape that's the same whether the model is Anthropic's Claude or Amazon's own Titan
A browsable catalog of first-party, partner, and open-weight models organized by provider
A dedicated, hourly-billed virtual machine that a model runs on
A severity-scoring system for moderating harmful content in prompts and responses
questions.explain: Bedrock's model picker already groups multiple providers behind one console. The Converse API goes a step further for the actual request shape itself: one unified call format works the same way regardless of which model-id (Anthropic, Amazon Titan, Meta, Mistral, and others) you point it at, instead of learning a different native request format per provider.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: Google's own documentation has rebranded Vertex AI's product area to the ________, although the console, SDK, and deployment pane you actually click through still say Vertex AI.
questions.explain: Per Lesson 18, Google's documentation rebranded this product area to Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform in 2026, but the console, SDK, and the Deploy on Vertex AI pane still use the name Vertex AI — which is also what most working engineers still say day to day.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the four questions Lesson 19 says actually decide a cloud AI platform choice.
options: Where the data already lives matters, since moving terabytes of documents or embeddings across clouds is slow and expensive
Which platform has the single best model this month is explicitly the top deciding factor
An existing AWS or GCP account with identity, networking, and billing already set up outweighs a model that's marginally better on paper
What the team already knows matters, because three clouds' worth of IAM quirks and CLI tools isn't free to learn on a deadline
Model exclusivity never matters, since every model eventually launches on every cloud
questions.explain: The four questions are: where's the data, who's already there (existing account/identity/billing), which models does each platform actually offer, and what does the team already know. Lesson 19 explicitly says 'which cloud has the best model' is NOT the deciding factor, since model quality converges fast across providers — and it names model exclusivity as one of the four real questions worth asking, not something to dismiss outright.

questions.code:
def ask_model(prompt: str) -> str:
    return provider_client.complete(prompt)
questions.prompt: Per Lesson 20, what does wrapping every model call in one function like this actually buy an application?
options: Swapping providers later means changing what's inside this one function, not hunting down every call site scattered across the app
It automatically translates prompts between different providers' request formats
It removes any need to read configuration from environment variables
It guarantees the response is faster by caching every call
questions.explain: The fix Lesson 20 describes is a seam, not a rewrite: one small function the rest of the app calls instead of importing a provider SDK directly everywhere. If the app ever needs to switch providers, only that one function's internals change — every other call site in the app stays untouched.

questions.prompt: Match each catalog or serving term to what it actually is, per Lessons 17-19.
right: Groups foundation models by provider — Amazon, Anthropic, Meta, Mistral, Cohere — behind one API
The managed service that actually deploys and serves a model chosen from Model Garden
Browse and deploy models from Azure OpenAI, Meta, Mistral, DeepSeek, and more, inside Foundry
Google's browsable catalog of first-party, partner, and open-weight models
questions.explain: Azure's model catalog lets you browse and deploy models from Azure OpenAI and partners inside Foundry. AWS Bedrock's model picker groups foundation models by provider behind one API. Google's Model Garden is the browsable catalog itself, while Vertex AI is the managed service that actually deploys and serves whatever you pick from it — the same catalog-versus-serving-layer split Azure and AWS both have too.

questions.prompt: Put these three things worth keeping portable from day one in the order Lesson 20 lists them.
items: Prompts kept in files or a prompt store, not buried inline inside SDK calls
Config — endpoint, key, and model name — read from environment variables, not hardcoded
Embeddings' dimension and distance metric noted explicitly
questions.explain: Lesson 20 names three cheap habits that keep a future cloud migration from being harder than it has to be: keep prompts out of inline SDK calls, read config from environment variables instead of hardcoding it, and note an embedding's dimension and distance metric explicitly, since not every provider's embedding model agrees on either one.

questions.prompt: A ManagedOnlineDeployment named capstone-deploy has just been created on an endpoint, but endpoint.traffic has not yet been set. Per Lesson 22, what percentage of requests does capstone-deploy receive at this point?
options: 0% — a fresh deployment starts at 0% traffic until it's explicitly routed to
100% — any single deployment on an endpoint automatically receives all its traffic
50% — traffic is split evenly across every deployment on an endpoint by default
Invoking the endpoint fails immediately until a traffic split is configured
questions.explain: An endpoint can host multiple deployments split by traffic percentage, but a fresh deployment gets 0% until it's explicitly routed to — which is exactly why Lesson 22's next line sets endpoint.traffic = {"capstone-deploy": 100} before anything will actually answer a request sent to the endpoint.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: checking the shared-quota checkbox in the Foundry deployment dialog borrows temporary quota instead of your own, but Microsoft automatically deletes that endpoint after ________ hours.
questions.explain: Lesson 21's shared-quota checkbox reads, in part, 'I acknowledge that this endpoint will be deleted in 168 hours' — borrowed quota in exchange for an automatic one-week teardown, a trade-off that actually favors a capstone you're going to screenshot, test, and tear down anyway.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about securing and monitoring the capstone endpoint, per Lesson 23.
options: Storing the endpoint's key in a Key Vault secret and reading it with DefaultAzureCredential() removes the need to paste a key anywhere a screen share or git log could expose it
az monitor diagnostic-settings create routes a resource's logs and metrics to a destination like a Log Analytics workspace
Running the diagnostic-settings command requires changing the application's own code
Disabling public network access is a setting specific to AI endpoints, not something other Azure resources support
Once the diagnostic setting is active, the same Foundry Monitor tab dashboard from Lesson 11 is where you'd watch the endpoint's token usage and latency over time
questions.explain: Storing the key in Key Vault and reading it with DefaultAzureCredential() means there's no key anywhere a screen share or git log could expose. The az monitor diagnostic-settings create command routes logs and metrics to Log Analytics with no application code change at all. And it's the same Monitor tab dashboard from Lesson 11 that shows the results once logs start flowing — this command family works identically against almost any Azure resource, not just AI endpoints.

questions.prompt: Match each capstone deliverable to the earlier lesson(s) it pulls its approach from, per Lesson 21.
right: Lesson 24 — naming a real limitation instead of claiming the deployment is flawless
Lesson 6 (SDK basics) and Lesson 7 (deploying a model endpoint)
Lesson 10 (cost management) and Lesson 11 (monitoring AI service usage)
Lesson 14 (networking) and Lesson 16 (managed identities & Key Vault)
questions.explain: The live endpoint deliverable pulls from Lesson 6's SDK basics and Lesson 7's deployment flow. The secured endpoint pulls from Lesson 14's networking and Lesson 16's managed identities and Key Vault. The monitored endpoint pulls from Lesson 10's cost management and Lesson 11's monitoring. And presenting the finished capstone, per Lesson 24, is about naming one real limitation rather than claiming the deployment is flawless.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of the capstone's SDK deployment path in the correct order, per Lesson 22.
items: Authenticate and connect to the Foundry project's workspace with MLClient
Create a ManagedOnlineEndpoint with a unique, timestamped name
Create a ManagedOnlineDeployment pointing at a model ID from the catalog
Route 100% of traffic to the new deployment
Invoke the endpoint and confirm a real response comes back
questions.explain: Lesson 22's SDK path runs in exactly this order: connect with MLClient and InteractiveBrowserCredential, create the endpoint container, create the deployment that actually runs inside it, explicitly route traffic to that deployment since a new one starts at 0%, and finally invoke the endpoint to confirm a real response — not an error or a timeout — comes back.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 24, why should a managed-compute capstone deployment be deleted once you've captured your screenshots, rather than left running?
options: A managed-compute deployment bills by the hour whether or not anyone is actually calling it
Azure automatically deletes every managed-compute deployment after exactly 24 hours regardless of how it was created
Leaving it running would cause its Target URI to stop resolving
The Foundry portal blocks starting a new capstone until the previous deployment is deleted
questions.explain: Lesson 10 already established that token-billed and compute-billed AI resources need active cost management, and Lesson 24 applies that directly to the capstone: a managed-compute deployment bills by the hour regardless of traffic, so once you have a screenshot of Succeeded and Healthy plus your diagnostic setting, deleting the deployment (or letting a shared-quota endpoint's 168-hour timer do it) is what keeps the bill from becoming a surprise.
